title: The Lantern Vigil
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
Severus stood beneath the far arch with his coat buttoned to the throat and his hands in his pockets.

I spotted him because everyone else was moving.

The Frostturn Lantern Walk had drawn people from every district, though not everyone had come for the same reason. Some carried lights painted with names. Some wore their best coats. Others had arrived straight from work, their boots still muddy from the ridge path. A child had brought a lantern shaped like an extremely unconvincing duck.

Greg was playing a slow instrumental piece near the fountain.

For once, he hadn't been asked to fill every silence. The notes sat lightly in the air, leaving spaces for the sound of water beneath the old stones. People could listen, talk quietly, or ignore the music altogether.

Severus was doing none of those things. He was watching the lanterns with an expression I couldn't read.

I started toward him.

Then I stopped.

We had spent months learning that affection did not make another person's solitude a problem for me to solve. It would be easy to walk over and decide his silence was an invitation simply because I wanted to be beside him.

I approached slowly enough that he could see me.

"Would you like company?" I asked.

He glanced at me.

"That depends."

"On?"

"Whether you intend to describe the emotional significance of every lantern."

"I was going to start with the duck."

He looked across the square.

"That creature is anatomically offensive."

I smiled.

"Can I stand here?"

He moved slightly to make room.

It was a small answer. It was enough.

We watched the procession begin. Neri checked the safe route, Edda directed people away from the steps still closed after the storm, and Pip made sure the temporary lantern stands did not narrow the walkway. The lower passage toward Tideglass remained under inspection. Nobody treated the festival as permission to ignore a closure.

Greg's song changed key.

Severus's fingers twitched inside his pocket.

"Do you know the piece?" I asked.

"No."

"Do you like it?"

He considered.

"It doesn't insist on being admired."

I laughed softly.

"Greg would probably consider that high praise."

"Then please don't tell him."

The air smelled of cold stone, candle smoke, and the citrus tea Iroh was serving from a stand near the bakery. A lantern moved past us carrying a painted blue wave. Another held no mark at all.

I thought of the third wartime letter Severus had chosen not to open.

"Are you remembering someone?" I asked, then immediately wished I'd phrased it differently.

He looked at me.

"Several people."

"You don't have to tell me who."

"I know."

We stood quietly.

After a while he said, "For much of my life, remembrance was a public examination. People expected grief to resemble guilt, or loyalty, or confession. They wanted a correct answer."

"And here?"

"Here there is a duck."

I snorted.

He glanced at me.

"An important improvement."

I covered my mouth.

He finally smiled.

A small disagreement interrupted the line before it reached the corner.

Two volunteers had placed a lantern stand across the paved turning space outside the tea stall. Nobody had done it carelessly; the wind was stronger there, and the stand looked secure against the wall. But Edda stopped when she reached it.

"I can't turn around that," she said.

One of the volunteers looked toward the steps.

"We can carry it past you."

"I don't need to be carried past it," Edda answered. "The stand needs to move."

Severus watched the conversation with his hands still in his pockets.

The volunteer flushed. "We thought the space was wide enough."

"Then measure it," Edda said.

Pip fetched the chalk and a ruler, and the group moved the stand to a spot where it could be safely tethered without narrowing the route. It took less than ten minutes. The rest of the procession simply waited, talking quietly while Greg played the last notes of his piece.

Severus tilted his head.

"They corrected the design without declaring anyone incompetent."

"You're sounding impressed."

"I am assessing an interesting deviation from school staff meetings."

I laughed.

He looked at Edda, who had resumed her place in the line on her own terms.

"When I taught," he said after a moment, "I sometimes mistook embarrassment for a useful lesson."

I let the admission stand. I could have asked for a list of his regrets. Instead I asked whether he wanted another cup of tea.

"Later," he said. "I should like to see whether this ridiculous bird-shaped lantern survives the wind."

It did. A child held it with both hands and grinned as though the survival was entirely their own achievement.

Severus allowed himself a small smile.

I loved that he had seen the practical work and what it meant, without needing the entire evening to become a public confession.

The child with the duck lantern stopped at the edge of the path. One side of the handle had bent, and the lantern hung at a sorry angle.

Severus went very still.

"Don't touch the hot frame," he said.

The child froze, eyes wide. I felt my own shoulders tighten at his tone. For one awful second I saw the old classroom, the sharp correction that could turn a mistake into shame.

Then he noticed the child's face.

"The handle," he said, more quietly. "Not you. The metal has come loose."

Edda came over to check whether anyone had been burned. Nobody had. She suggested taking the lantern to the repair table before anyone tried to carry it again.

Severus crouched, though his knees clearly objected.

"Would you permit me to examine it once it cools?"

The child nodded, then looked at me. I didn't speak for them. I moved closer to the repair table so they could see where the lantern would go.

Greg's music stopped across the square. Not dramatically; he had simply finished his agreed set. The absence made it easier to hear Severus explain to the child which little tab had bent and why nobody should try to straighten it while it was hot.

"You sound like a teacher," I said when the child had gone to find their family.

"A deplorable habit."

"Not always."

He looked at me sharply, expecting mockery. I didn't give him any. I had watched him change the sentence before it became a wound. I couldn't know what it cost him, but I had seen him do it.

"Are you pleased with yourself?" I asked.

"Not particularly."

"Then perhaps I am pleased with you."

He looked away. Under the hem of his cloak his fingers found mine, briefly and without show.

"An intolerable distinction," he muttered.

We stayed until the lantern cooled. When the child returned, the repair worker—not Severus—decided whether it was safe to lift again. Severus accepted that without a single argument. The duck wobbled happily away, its lopsided light shining on the stones.

The procession moved toward Jasmine Steps. Greg stopped playing and helped carry a lantern stand to the next corner. He had volunteered for one shift, not an entire night of unpaid music. I watched him exchange a few words with Iroh, then return to the square without a guitar in his hands.

Severus followed my gaze.

"Your other companions appear to be managing."

"They are."

He nodded.

I waited for the old sharp remark. It didn't come.

We had spoken about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory often enough that he no longer treated every shared public event as a test of whether I would choose him above someone else. But understanding didn't erase the need for small negotiations.

"Do you want to walk with me?" I asked. "Or would you rather stay here?"

He looked down the lit path.

"Walk. Slowly."

We joined the back of the procession. Nobody asked him to carry a lantern. Nobody tried to make him speak about the war. We passed the workshop lights at Brasswatch, then turned toward the safe ridge above Tideglass.

Maui was helping a family settle blankets onto a bench, making a ridiculous show of lifting the entire stack one-handed. He spotted us, swept into a mock bow from a respectful distance, then let the family decide where the last blanket belonged. He didn't call us over.

Severus noticed.

"He's learning restraint."

"Painfully."

"A remarkable achievement."

I smiled.

At the cove, I hung a small lantern with an open amber circle beside the others. It wasn't mine to explain. Severus watched me place it on the hook and step back.

"You left it blank," he said.

"Not blank. Unnamed."

He considered that distinction.

"Very well."

He took a folded scrap of paper from his pocket. I pretended not to notice until he held it out.

It was a single line, written in his precise handwriting.

FOR THOSE I FAILED TO ASK.

I looked at him.

"You want this on a lantern?"

"No." His voice was quiet. "I wanted you to know I had something to say. I don't want it displayed."

I folded the paper carefully and gave it back.

"Then it's yours."

He closed his fingers around it.

The wind off the sea was colder than it had been in the square. I shivered. Without comment, Severus opened the side of his cloak and drew me close enough to share its shelter.

"Is this acceptable?" he asked.

"Very."

He looked down at me.

"You appear to be smiling."

"I am."

"An unwise reaction to such an undignified arrangement."

"Extremely."

His hand rested against my back. He leaned close, paused, and let me close the last distance myself. The kiss was quiet enough to belong to us, not the crowd.

When we turned toward the path, Greg began another instrumental somewhere beyond the ridge.

Severus listened for a moment.

"Tell him," he said reluctantly, "that the second piece was better."

"Would you like to tell him yourself?"

He looked offended.

"Don't become ambitious."

I laughed.

The night ended without a speech from Severus, a public confession, or a declaration that he'd been transformed by festival lights.

He walked home beside me, our hands brushing inside the shelter of his cloak.

I didn't need the silence to mean anything more than he had chosen to share it.
